The evaluation provides only a limited comparison of model performance. With two forecast years, individual errors have a large influence on the accuracy measures. A model that performs well for these observations may behave differently over a longer period.

The naïve model achieved the lowest RMSE and MAE, indicating that using the latest observed GPU demand produced smaller errors than extending a trend during this short evaluation. However, this result does not establish that GPU demand will remain constant or that the naïve method is suitable for forecasting through 2030.

@tbl-gpu-accuracy reports the calculated accuracy results for the four models.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-gpu-accuracy
#| tbl-cap: "Exploratory rolling-origin forecast accuracy for GPU demand, 2025–2026."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

gpu_accuracy <- gpu_cv_long |>
  dplyr::group_by(model) |>
  dplyr::summarise(
    RMSE = sqrt(
      mean((actual - forecast)^2)
    ),
    MAE = mean(
      abs(actual - forecast)
    ),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  dplyr::arrange(RMSE) |>
  dplyr::mutate(
    `RMSE rank` = dplyr::row_number()
  )

gpu_accuracy_table <- gpu_accuracy |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    Model = as.character(model),
    `RMSE (million GPU-hours)` = round(RMSE, 3),
    `MAE (million GPU-hours)` = round(MAE, 3),
    `RMSE rank` = `RMSE rank`
  )

knitr::kable(
  gpu_accuracy_table,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

The naïve benchmark achieved the lowest RMSE (0.441 million GPU-hours) and MAE (0.353 million GPU-hours), followed by drift, log-linear trend and linear trend. Unlike the overall HPC and CPU evaluations, the simpler benchmark performed better than the models estimating historical growth.

Figure 7 shows that all four models underestimated GPU demand in 2026. The naïve model projected approximately 2.39 million GPU-hours, compared with the estimated value of 3.00 million GPU-hours. The trend models also failed to anticipate this increase. This illustrates the difficulty of forecasting GPU demand when the historical series contains substantial changes over a short period.

The accuracy rankings should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously. Only two forecast errors were available for each model, and the underlying GPU-hour series includes derived estimates and conversion assumptions. Consequently, the evaluation does not provide sufficient evidence to establish that the naïve model will remain the most accurate approach over a longer forecast horizon.

The naïve model was retained as a reference because of its lower evaluation errors. Linear and log-linear models were also retained to examine the consequences of different growth assumptions. However, none of these models was selected as a reliable central GPU forecast.

Following the project review, GPU projections were treated as exploratory and excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios. Those scenarios instead use the selected overall HPC demand projection and historical Field of Research allocation shares. This distinction prevents the more uncertain GPU estimates from being presented as independently validated planning requirements.

The exploratory GPU projections are presented in Section 4.3 to show how different modelling assumptions affect the results through 2030. More consistent historical records of GPU requests, allocations and usage, together with validated conversion factors, would be needed to support reliable GPU-specific forecasting.


### Residual Diagnostics

The rolling-origin evaluation assessed how accurately the forecasting models predicted observations excluded from their training samples. Residual diagnostics were then conducted on the selected linear trend models for overall HPC and CPU demand, using the complete 2014–2026 historical series.

The purpose was to examine whether the fitted models left systematic patterns in their errors and whether their residual distributions supported the assumptions used to construct statistical prediction intervals.

Residual autocorrelation was examined using the autocorrelation function (ACF) and the Ljung–Box test. Normal Q–Q plots were also examined to assess departures from the normal-error assumption. These diagnostics complement the out-of-sample evaluation presented in Sections 4.2.1 and 4.2.2.

Figure @fig-model-diagnostics presents the residual diagnostics for both selected models.

```{r}
#| label: fig-model-diagnostics
#| fig-cap: "Residual diagnostics for the selected linear trend models fitted to 2014–2026: residual ACF and normal Q–Q plots for overall HPC and CPU demand."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 7
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)
library(patchwork)

# Prepare the historical series used for forecasting
hpc_diagnostic_data <- annual_analysis |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand = as.numeric(demand_ksu)
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

cpu_diagnostic_data <- annual_converted |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    demand = as.numeric(demand_cpu_core_hours) / 1e6
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(hpc_diagnostic_data$year, 2014:2026),
  identical(cpu_diagnostic_data$year, 2014:2026),
  all(is.finite(hpc_diagnostic_data$demand)),
  all(is.finite(cpu_diagnostic_data$demand))
)

# Fit selected linear trend models using all 13 observations
hpc_diagnostic_fit <- lm(
  demand ~ year,
  data = hpc_diagnostic_data
)

cpu_diagnostic_fit <- lm(
  demand ~ year,
  data = cpu_diagnostic_data
)

# Function for residual ACF plots
make_acf_plot <- function(model, title) {

  residual_values <- residuals(model)

  acf_result <- acf(
    residual_values,
    plot = FALSE,
    lag.max = 5
  )

  acf_data <- tibble(
    lag = as.numeric(acf_result$lag)[-1],
    autocorrelation = as.numeric(acf_result$acf)[-1]
  )

  # Approximate reference limits, not a formal
  # hypothesis test for individual residual lags
  confidence_limit <- 1.96 / sqrt(length(residual_values))

  ggplot(
    acf_data,
    aes(
      x = lag,
      y = autocorrelation
    )
  ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = 0,
      colour = "#555555"
    ) +
    geom_hline(
      yintercept = c(
        -confidence_limit,
        confidence_limit
      ),
      colour = "#CC6677",
      linetype = "dashed",
      linewidth = 0.6
    ) +
    geom_segment(
      aes(
        xend = lag,
        yend = 0
      ),
      colour = "#0077A8",
      linewidth = 1
    ) +
    geom_point(
      colour = "#0077A8",
      size = 2
    ) +
    scale_x_continuous(
      breaks = 1:5
    ) +
    coord_cartesian(
      ylim = c(-1, 1)
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Lag (years)",
      y = "Residual ACF"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# Function for normal Q-Q plots
make_qq_plot <- function(model, title) {

  residual_data <- tibble(
    residual = as.numeric(residuals(model))
  )

  ggplot(
    residual_data,
    aes(sample = residual)
  ) +
    stat_qq(
      colour = "#0077A8",
      size = 2
    ) +
    stat_qq_line(
      colour = "#CC6677",
      linewidth = 0.8
    ) +
    labs(
      title = title,
      x = "Theoretical quantiles",
      y = "Residual quantiles"
    ) +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 10) +
    theme(
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
    )
}

# Create four diagnostic panels
p_hpc_acf <- make_acf_plot(
  hpc_diagnostic_fit,
  "A. HPC residual ACF"
)

p_hpc_qq <- make_qq_plot(
  hpc_diagnostic_fit,
  "B. HPC normal Q-Q plot"
)

p_cpu_acf <- make_acf_plot(
  cpu_diagnostic_fit,
  "C. CPU residual ACF"
)

p_cpu_qq <- make_qq_plot(
  cpu_diagnostic_fit,
  "D. CPU normal Q-Q plot"
)

(p_hpc_acf | p_hpc_qq) /
  (p_cpu_acf | p_cpu_qq) +
  plot_annotation(
    caption = paste(
      "Diagnostics use in-sample residuals from",
      "linear trend models fitted to 2014–2026.",
      "Dashed ACF lines are approximate reference limits.",
      "CPU residuals are measured in million core-hours."
    )
  )
```

The residual ACF plots show relatively small correlations for both models. None of the displayed correlations exceeds the approximate reference limits.

For overall HPC demand, the residual correlations are close to zero across most displayed lags. This suggests that the linear trend captures much of the systematic movement in the historical series, although the short sample limits the strength of this conclusion.

CPU residuals show a more noticeable negative correlation at lag 1 and lag 4. These correlations remain within the approximate reference limits, but they indicate that some year-to-year variation may not be fully captured by a single linear trend.

The Ljung–Box test was used to examine whether the residual autocorrelations were jointly distinguishable from zero over the first three lags. Table @tbl-ljung-box reports the results.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ljung-box
#| tbl-cap: "Ljung–Box tests of residual autocorrelation for the selected linear trend models, using three lags."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

diagnostic_lag <- 3

# No ARMA error terms were fitted.
# fitdf = 0 retains the three test degrees of freedom.
hpc_lb <- Box.test(
  residuals(hpc_diagnostic_fit),
  lag = diagnostic_lag,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

cpu_lb <- Box.test(
  residuals(cpu_diagnostic_fit),
  lag = diagnostic_lag,
  type = "Ljung-Box",
  fitdf = 0
)

diagnostic_results <- tibble(
  `Demand measure` = c(
    "Overall HPC",
    "CPU"
  ),
  `Ljung-Box statistic` = c(
    unname(hpc_lb$statistic),
    unname(cpu_lb$statistic)
  ),
  `Lag` = diagnostic_lag,
  `Degrees of freedom` = c(
    unname(hpc_lb$parameter),
    unname(cpu_lb$parameter)
  ),
  `p-value` = c(
    hpc_lb$p.value,
    cpu_lb$p.value
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    `Ljung-Box statistic` = round(
      `Ljung-Box statistic`, 3
    ),
    `p-value` = round(
      `p-value`, 3
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  diagnostic_results,
  align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

The Ljung–Box results do not provide sufficient evidence to reject the null hypothesis of no residual autocorrelation at the tested lags for either selected model, using a 5% significance level.

However, the results should not be interpreted as proof that the residuals are independent. Each model was fitted using only 13 annual observations, and the test has limited power with such a small sample. The ACF reference limits are also approximate.

The normal Q–Q plots provide additional information about the distribution of the fitted errors.

For overall HPC demand, most residuals lie reasonably close to the theoretical reference line, although some departures are visible around the centre and upper tail. The plot does not show an obvious severe departure from normality, but the small sample makes the distribution difficult to assess reliably.

The CPU Q–Q plot shows more noticeable departures, particularly in the lower tail. The most negative residual falls substantially below the reference line, suggesting that the normal-error assumption may be less suitable for CPU demand.

These differences matter when interpreting model-based prediction intervals. The intervals depend on assumptions about the fitted error distribution, and departures from those assumptions may affect their coverage. The CPU intervals therefore require particular caution.

Overall, the diagnostics do not reveal strong evidence of residual autocorrelation in the selected linear models. However, they do not establish that the fitted trends or their error distributions will remain unchanged through 2030.

The residual diagnostics support the use of the linear models as interpretable forecasting references, while reinforcing the need to consider alternative growth assumptions and sensitivity to the 2026 observation. These issues are examined in Section 4.3.

### Evaluation Summary

The rolling-origin evaluation identified different forecasting results for overall HPC, CPU and GPU demand. The model selection considered forecast accuracy, historical data coverage, growth assumptions and the reliability of the underlying observations.

For **overall HPC demand**, the linear trend achieved the lowest RMSE (290,898 kSU) and MAE (198,295 kSU) across six evaluation years. Its RMSE was 23.2% lower than the naïve benchmark, although the improvement over drift was smaller at 7.5%. The linear model was therefore selected as the central forecasting model, with drift providing a useful benchmark. The log-linear model was retained as an alternative growth scenario despite its weaker historical accuracy.

For **CPU demand**, the results were less decisive. The linear trend achieved the lowest RMSE (157.72 million core-hours), while the log-linear model achieved the lowest MAE (133.74 million core-hours). The difference in RMSE between the two models was only 1.5%. The linear model was selected for the central projection because it provided competitive accuracy and assumed a constant annual increase rather than continued proportional growth. The log-linear model was retained to examine how this alternative assumption affects demand through 2030.

Both selected linear models were sensitive to the latest observation. Including 2026 increased the estimated annual growth by 12.2% for overall HPC demand and 11.9% for CPU demand. This supported retaining forecasts excluding 2026 as sensitivity comparisons, rather than relying only on models fitted to the complete historical series.

Residual diagnostics provided no strong evidence of autocorrelation in either selected linear model. However, the Ljung–Box tests had limited power with 13 annual observations. The CPU Q–Q plot also showed departures from normality, particularly in the lower tail. These findings indicate that statistical prediction intervals should be interpreted cautiously, especially for CPU demand.

For **GPU demand**, the naïve benchmark achieved the lowest RMSE (0.441 million GPU-hours) and MAE (0.353 million GPU-hours). However, the evaluation used only two forecast years, and the underlying GPU-hour series depended partly on conversion assumptions. These results were insufficient to select a reliable long-term forecasting model. Following the project review, GPU projections were retained for exploratory analysis but excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios.

Overall, the evaluation supports using the **linear trend as the central reference for overall HPC and CPU demand**, while retaining alternative growth assumptions and models excluding 2026 to examine forecast sensitivity. The initial national HPC planning scenarios are based on the overall HPC projection and historical Field of Research allocation shares. Section 4.3 presents these projections and examines how the modelling assumptions affect the results through 2030.

## Demand Forecasts to 2030


### Overall HPC Demand

The rolling-origin evaluation in Section 4.2.1 identified the linear trend as the most accurate of the four models for overall HPC demand. The model was therefore fitted to the complete 2014–2026 series to generate the central projections for 2027–2030.

Three alternative specifications were retained to examine how the projections depend on the historical observations and growth assumptions. The first excludes 2026 from the linear model to assess the influence of the latest observation. The other two use log-linear trends, fitted with and without 2026, to examine the implications of continued proportional growth.

This comparison is important because recorded HPC requests increased sharply in 2026. Including this observation increased the estimated annual linear growth from approximately 144,357 to 161,992 kSU, or 12.2%. The alternative specifications therefore assess the sensitivity of the 2030 projections to both the latest observation and the assumed growth pattern.

@fig-hpc-forecast-scenarios connects the historical observations with the four projected trajectories. The 2030 values are labelled to show the differences between the forecasting assumptions.

```{r}
#| label: fig-hpc-forecast-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "Historical HPC demand and alternative projections to 2030. The full-history linear model provides the central forecast. Alternative trajectories show sensitivity to the 2026 observation and growth assumptions."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Prepare historical HPC demand
hpc_model_data <- annual_analysis |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    time = as.integer(year) - 2014,
    demand_ksu = as.numeric(demand_ksu)
  ) |>
  arrange(year)

stopifnot(
  identical(hpc_model_data$year, 2014:2026),
  all(is.finite(hpc_model_data$demand_ksu)),
  all(hpc_model_data$demand_ksu > 0)
)

# Data excluding the latest observation
hpc_model_pre2026 <- hpc_model_data |>
  filter(year <= 2025)

# Fit four model specifications
overall_linear <- lm(
  demand_ksu ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_data
)

overall_linear_pre2026 <- lm(
  demand_ksu ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_pre2026
)

overall_loglinear <- lm(
  log(demand_ksu) ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_data
)

overall_loglinear_pre2026 <- lm(
  log(demand_ksu) ~ time,
  data = hpc_model_pre2026
)

# Historical observations
hpc_history <- hpc_model_data |>
  transmute(
    year,
    demand_m = demand_ksu / 1e6
  )

# Include 2026 as a fitted anchor
# and 2027–2030 as forecast years
hpc_projection_years <- tibble(
  year = 2026:2030,
  time = (2026:2030) - 2014
)

# Generate four scenario trajectories
hpc_scenario_wide <- hpc_projection_years |>
  transmute(
    year,
    `Central linear` = as.numeric(
      predict(
        overall_linear,
        newdata = hpc_projection_years
      )
    ) / 1e6,
    `Linear excluding 2026` = as.numeric(
      predict(
        overall_linear_pre2026,
        newdata = hpc_projection_years
      )
    ) / 1e6,
    `Log-linear full history` = exp(
      as.numeric(
        predict(
          overall_loglinear,
          newdata = hpc_projection_years
        )
      )
    ) / 1e6,
    `Log-linear excluding 2026` = exp(
      as.numeric(
        predict(
          overall_loglinear_pre2026,
          newdata = hpc_projection_years
        )
      )
    ) / 1e6
  )

scenario_levels <- c(
  "Central linear",
  "Linear excluding 2026",
  "Log-linear full history",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026"
)

hpc_scenario_long <- hpc_scenario_wide |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -year,
    names_to = "scenario",
    values_to = "demand_m"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    scenario = factor(
      scenario,
      levels = scenario_levels
    )
  )

# Label the four 2030 endpoints
hpc_end_labels <- hpc_scenario_long |>
  filter(year == 2030) |>
  mutate(
    label = sprintf("%.2f", demand_m)
  )

scenario_colours <- c(
  "Central linear" = "#0077A8",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "#64748B",
  "Log-linear full history" = "#D97706",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "#B91C1C"
)

scenario_linetypes <- c(
  "Central linear" = "solid",
  "Linear excluding 2026" = "dashed",
  "Log-linear full history" = "dotdash",
  "Log-linear excluding 2026" = "longdash"
)

ggplot() +
  annotate(
    "rect",
    xmin = 2026.5,
    xmax = 2030.7,
    ymin = -Inf,
    ymax = Inf,
    fill = "#EFF5F9",
    alpha = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = hpc_history,
    aes(x = year, y = demand_m),
    colour = "#173A5E",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = hpc_history,
    aes(x = year, y = demand_m),
    colour = "#173A5E",
    size = 1.8
  ) +
  geom_line(
    data = hpc_scenario_long,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      colour = scenario,
      linetype = scenario,
      group = scenario
    ),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  geom_point(
    data = filter(
      hpc_scenario_long,
      year >= 2027
    ),
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      colour = scenario
    ),
    size = 2
  ) +
  geom_text(
    data = hpc_end_labels,
    aes(
      x = year,
      y = demand_m,
      label = label,
      colour = scenario
    ),
    hjust = -0.3,
    size = 3.3,
    fontface = "bold",
    show.legend = FALSE
  ) +
  geom_vline(
    xintercept = 2026.5,
    linetype = "dotted",
    colour = "#64748B"
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(
    values = scenario_colours
  ) +
  scale_linetype_manual(
    values = scenario_linetypes
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = c(
      2014, 2016, 2018, 2020,
      2022, 2024, 2026,
      2027, 2028, 2029, 2030
    ),
    limits = c(2014, 2031),
    expand = expansion(mult = 0.01)
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(accuracy = 0.1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.03, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Year",
    y = "HPC demand (million kSU)",
    colour = NULL,
    linetype = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Shading indicates the projection period.",
      "Scenario lines begin at fitted 2026 values,",
      "not necessarily observed 2026 demand.",
      "Alternative scenarios are not prediction interval bounds."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 9),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8)
  ) +
  guides(
    colour = guide_legend(ncol = 2),
    linetype = guide_legend(ncol = 2)
  )
```

The central linear model projects approximately 2.02 million kSU in 2027, increasing by around 161,992 kSU annually to reach 2.50 million kSU in 2030. This represents an increase of approximately 11.6% from the reconstructed 2026 demand of 2.24 million kSU.

Excluding the 2026 observation reduces the 2030 projection to approximately 2.29 million kSU, around 210,000 kSU below the central forecast. This difference shows that the latest observation influences the estimated growth rate, even when the same linear model is used.

The full-history log-linear model produces a substantially higher 2030 projection of approximately 6.48 million kSU. Unlike the linear model, which assumes a constant absolute annual increase, the log-linear model extends proportional growth. As a result, its projected annual increases become progressively larger.

However, the log-linear model recorded the highest RMSE and MAE during the rolling-origin evaluation in Section 4.2.1. Its higher projection is therefore retained to illustrate sensitivity to the growth assumption, rather than as an equally supported central forecast or a validated upper limit.

For planning purposes, the difference between the linear and log-linear projections is more substantial than the difference caused by excluding 2026. This indicates that the assumed growth pattern has a greater influence on the 2030 estimate than the latest observation alone. The linear model is therefore retained as the central reference, while the alternative trajectories illustrate how different assumptions affect the longer-term outlook.

These projections describe recorded HPC requests rather than unconstrained researcher demand. They provide a basis for considering future national computing requirements, but should not be interpreted as precise estimates of the capacity that facilities will need to provide. The statistical uncertainty around the selected central forecast is examined separately in Section 4.3.2.

#### Prediction Intervals and Forecast Uncertainty

The differences between forecasting scenarios describe uncertainty arising from model selection and historical data. Statistical prediction intervals address a different question: how much future annual demand might vary around the selected linear trend if the fitted model and its error assumptions remain appropriate.

Figure @fig-hpc-forecast-intervals shows the central projection with 80% and 95% model-based prediction intervals.


```{r}
#| label: fig-hpc-forecast-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Central HPC demand projection with 80% and 95% model-based prediction intervals, 2027–2030. Intervals are conditional on the fitted linear model."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Use the selected full-history linear trend model
# fitted to 2014–2026 in Section 4.3.1.
stopifnot(
  exists("overall_linear"),
  inherits(overall_linear, "lm")
)

# Define future years using the same time index
# as the fitted model.
hpc_future <- tibble(
  year = 2027:2030,
  time = (2027:2030) - 2014
)

# Calculate 80% prediction intervals
hpc_pi_80 <- predict(
  overall_linear,
  newdata = hpc_future,
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.80
)

# Calculate 95% prediction intervals
hpc_pi_95 <- predict(
  overall_linear,
  newdata = hpc_future,
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.95
)

# Combine forecasts and interval bounds
# Convert kSU to million kSU for plotting.
hpc_intervals <- tibble(
  year = hpc_future$year,
  forecast = hpc_pi_95[, "fit"] / 1e6,
  lower_80 = hpc_pi_80[, "lwr"] / 1e6,
  upper_80 = hpc_pi_80[, "upr"] / 1e6,
  lower_95 = hpc_pi_95[, "lwr"] / 1e6,
  upper_95 = hpc_pi_95[, "upr"] / 1e6
)

# Verify that the intervals are correctly ordered
stopifnot(
  all(hpc_intervals$lower_95 <= hpc_intervals$lower_80),
  all(hpc_intervals$lower_80 <= hpc_intervals$forecast),
  all(hpc_intervals$forecast <= hpc_intervals$upper_80),
  all(hpc_intervals$upper_80 <= hpc_intervals$upper_95)
)

# Plot the selected forecast and uncertainty bands
ggplot(
  hpc_intervals,
  aes(x = year)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = lower_95,
      ymax = upper_95
    ),
    fill = "#B9D9EA",
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = lower_80,
      ymax = upper_80
    ),
    fill = "#5FA7CD",
    alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = forecast),
    colour = "#0077A8",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = forecast),
    colour = "#0077A8",
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      y = forecast,
      label = sprintf("%.2f", forecast)
    ),
    vjust = -1,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    colour = "#173A5E"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2027:2030
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_number(
      accuracy = 0.1
    ),
    expand = expansion(
      mult = c(0.08, 0.12)
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Forecast year",
    y = "HPC demand (million kSU)",
    caption = paste(
      "Darker band: 80% prediction interval.",
      "Lighter band: 95% prediction interval.",
      "Intervals exclude uncertainty from alternative model specifications."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(
      size = 8
    )
  )
```

The selected linear model projects approximately 2.50 million kSU in 2030, with a 95% prediction interval of approximately 1.98–3.03 million kSU. The interval is substantially wider than the annual increase estimated by the model, showing that uncertainty remains important even when the central trend is relatively stable.

These intervals depend on the linear regression assumptions and the historical series used to fit the model. They do not account for possible changes in computing technology, reporting practices, research funding or the underlying relationship between requested and actual computing requirements.

The residual diagnostics in Section 4.2.4 provide some evidence about the fitted model's assumptions, but the short annual series limits how confidently these assumptions can be extended through 2030.

Overall, the linear model provides a transparent central estimate of approximately 2.50 million kSU for national HPC planning in 2030. The model excluding 2026 demonstrates sensitivity to the latest observation, while the log-linear alternatives show how different growth assumptions can produce much larger projections. These results should be interpreted as conditional planning estimates rather than precise future capacity requirements.



### CPU Demand

The rolling-origin evaluation in Section 4.2.2 showed that the linear and log-linear models performed similarly when forecasting CPU demand. The linear model achieved the lowest RMSE of 157.72 million core-hours, while the log-linear model achieved the lowest MAE of 133.74 million core-hours. The linear trend was selected as the central model because it provided competitive accuracy without assuming continued compounded growth.

The selected model was fitted to the complete 2014–2026 CPU series to generate projections for 2027–2030. Three alternative specifications were retained: a linear model excluding 2026, and log-linear models fitted with and without 2026. These alternatives examine the effects of the latest observation and different growth assumptions.

The 2026 observation is important because including it increased the estimated annual linear growth from approximately 72.41 million to 81.01 million core-hours, or 11.9%. With only 13 annual observations, the latest data can influence the estimated trend and projections several years ahead. @fig-cpu-forecast-scenarios compares the historical CPU demand series with the four projected trajectories.

```{r}
scenario_colours <- c(
```

The central linear model projects CPU demand of approximately 1.13 billion core-hours in 2027, increasing by around 81.01 million core-hours annually to reach 1.37 billion core-hours in 2030. This represents an increase of approximately 10.9% from the reconstructed 2026 CPU demand.

Excluding the 2026 observation reduces the 2030 projection to approximately 1.26 billion core-hours, around 106 million core-hours below the central forecast. This difference indicates that the latest observation has a noticeable influence on the fitted trend. With only 13 annual observations, changes in the latest data can affect projections several years ahead.

The full-history log-linear model produces a substantially higher projection of approximately 2.48 billion core-hours in 2030. This is approximately 81% higher than the central linear projection for the same year, despite the two models achieving similar accuracy during the one-year-ahead evaluation period. The difference arises because the log-linear model extends proportional growth, while the linear model assumes a constant absolute annual increase.

The two log-linear specifications also produce relatively similar projections when 2026 is included or excluded. This contrasts with the linear models, where excluding 2026 has a more noticeable effect on the 2030 projection. The comparison suggests that the log-linear CPU projections are less sensitive to the latest observation, although both depend on the assumption of continued proportional growth.

Unlike overall HPC demand, the log-linear CPU model performed competitively during rolling-origin evaluation. Its RMSE was approximately 1.5% higher than the linear model, while its MAE was approximately 3.5% lower. Therefore, the higher log-linear projection cannot be dismissed on the basis of historical forecast accuracy alone.

However, similar one-year-ahead accuracy does not establish that proportional growth will continue through 2030. The difference between the linear and log-linear projections illustrates how model assumptions become increasingly important over longer forecast horizons.

The linear model was retained as the central planning reference because it achieved the lowest RMSE and provides a more conservative and interpretable projection. The log-linear alternatives were retained to examine the implications of continued proportional growth rather than treated as equally likely outcomes.

#### CPU Prediction Intervals

The alternative CPU projections illustrate uncertainty associated with model selection and the inclusion of the 2026 observation. Prediction intervals address a different source of uncertainty by estimating how future observations may vary around the selected linear trend, assuming its statistical assumptions remain appropriate.

@fig-cpu-forecast-intervals presents the central CPU forecast with 80% and 95% prediction intervals for 2027–2030.

```{r}
#| label: fig-cpu-forecast-intervals
#| fig-cap: "Central CPU demand projection with 80% and 95% model-based prediction intervals, 2027–2030. Intervals are conditional on the fitted linear model."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.2
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

# Use the selected CPU linear model from the previous chunk
stopifnot(
  exists("cpu_linear"),
  inherits(cpu_linear, "lm")
)

# Future years, using the same model time index
cpu_future <- tibble(
  year = 2027:2030,
  time = (2027:2030) - 2014
)

# Calculate model-based prediction intervals
cpu_pi_80 <- predict(
  cpu_linear,
  newdata = cpu_future,
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.80
)

cpu_pi_95 <- predict(
  cpu_linear,
  newdata = cpu_future,
  interval = "prediction",
  level = 0.95
)

# Combine forecasts and interval bounds
cpu_intervals <- tibble(
  year = cpu_future$year,
  forecast = cpu_pi_95[, "fit"],
  lower_80 = cpu_pi_80[, "lwr"],
  upper_80 = cpu_pi_80[, "upr"],
  lower_95 = cpu_pi_95[, "lwr"],
  upper_95 = cpu_pi_95[, "upr"]
)

stopifnot(
  all(cpu_intervals$lower_95 <= cpu_intervals$lower_80),
  all(cpu_intervals$lower_80 <= cpu_intervals$forecast),
  all(cpu_intervals$forecast <= cpu_intervals$upper_80),
  all(cpu_intervals$upper_80 <= cpu_intervals$upper_95)
)

ggplot(
  cpu_intervals,
  aes(x = year)
) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = lower_95,
      ymax = upper_95
    ),
    fill = "#B9D9EA",
    alpha = 0.65
  ) +
  geom_ribbon(
    aes(
      ymin = lower_80,
      ymax = upper_80
    ),
    fill = "#5FA7CD",
    alpha = 0.55
  ) +
  geom_line(
    aes(y = forecast),
    colour = "#0077A8",
    linewidth = 1.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(y = forecast),
    colour = "#0077A8",
    size = 2.8
  ) +
  geom_text(
    aes(
      y = forecast,
      label = comma(round(forecast))
    ),
    vjust = -1,
    size = 3.5,
    fontface = "bold",
    colour = "#173A5E"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = 2027:2030
  ) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    labels = label_comma(accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.08, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Forecast year",
    y = "CPU demand (million core-hours)",
    caption = paste(
      "Darker band: 80% prediction interval.",
      "Lighter band: 95% prediction interval.",
      "Intervals exclude uncertainty from alternative model specifications."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8)
  )
```

The selected linear model projects approximately 1,369.90 million CPU core-hours in 2030, with a 95% prediction interval of approximately 974.24–1,765.55 million core-hours. The interval is relatively wide compared with the estimated annual increase of 81.01 million core-hours, indicating substantial uncertainty around individual future observations.

These intervals are conditional on the fitted linear model. They do not account for additional uncertainty associated with historical resource conversions, changes in computing infrastructure, reporting practices or alternative growth assumptions.

The full-history log-linear projection of approximately 2.48 billion core-hours lies well above the central model's 95% prediction interval. This does not invalidate either model. Instead, it demonstrates that a prediction interval calculated from one model does not capture the different outcomes produced by alternative model specifications.

The residual diagnostics in Section 4.2.4 provide additional information about the fitted model assumptions. However, the limited number of annual observations and historical reporting differences mean that the statistical intervals should be interpreted cautiously.

The central CPU forecast provides a reference for assessing future computing demand, while the alternative trajectories show how projections change under different growth assumptions. The large difference between the linear and log-linear projections indicates that planning decisions should consider more than one possible growth path. These CPU estimates should also be interpreted alongside overall HPC demand, rather than added together, because they represent related measures of computing requirements.


### GPU Demand

Unlike overall HPC and CPU demand, no central GPU forecasting model was selected. Formal prediction intervals were not reported because the five-year modelling series and uncertainty in the underlying estimates provided insufficient evidence for reliable statistical intervals.

Following the project review, GPU projections were retained as exploratory findings and excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios. Those scenarios instead use the selected overall HPC demand projection and historical Field of Research allocation shares.

The GPU results nevertheless highlight an important limitation for future planning. More consistent records of GPU requests, allocations, usage and hardware configurations would be needed to support reliable GPU-specific forecasts. Until such data become available, the projections should be used to examine modelling sensitivity rather than estimate future national GPU capacity requirements.

Figure @fig-gpu-forecast-scenarios shows the historical GPU demand estimates and the five exploratory trajectories through 2030.

```{r}

library(dplyr)

# --------------------------------------------------

stopifnot(

  filter(year == 2026) |>

# --------------------------------------------------

gpu_future <- data.frame(
  year = 2027:2030,
  time = (2027:2030) - 2022
)

gpu_scenarios <- gpu_future |>
  transmute(
    year,

        predict(

        )
      )
    ),

    `Log-linear excluding 2026` = exp(
      as.numeric(
        predict(

stopifnot(
  identical(gpu_scenarios$year, 2027:2030),
  all(is.finite(as.matrix(gpu_scenarios[, -1]))),
  all(as.matrix(gpu_scenarios[, -1]) > 0)
)

# Check the 2030 results against Chapter 10.
gpu_expected_2030 <- c(
  `Naïve benchmark` = 3.003,
  `Linear including 2026` = 3.371,
  `Linear excluding 2026` = 2.252,
  `Log-linear including 2026` = 3.681,
  `Log-linear excluding 2026` = 2.406
)

gpu_actual_2030 <- unlist(
  gpu_scenarios[
    gpu_scenarios$year == 2030,

if (any(

gpu_colours <- c(

ggplot() +
```

The five scenarios produce different estimates of GPU demand in 2030. The naïve benchmark maintains the latest estimated demand at approximately 3.00 million GPU-hours. The full-history linear model projects 3.37 million GPU-hours, while the full-history log-linear model projects 3.68 million GPU-hours.

Excluding 2026 produces substantially lower projections. The linear model excluding 2026 projects approximately 2.25 million GPU-hours in 2030, while the corresponding log-linear model projects 2.41 million GPU-hours.

The difference between the two linear specifications is approximately 1.12 million GPU-hours in 2030. The full-history linear projection is around 49.7% higher than the projection excluding 2026. This shows that the latest observation has a substantial influence on the estimated growth trajectory.

Across the five scenarios, the 2030 estimates range from approximately 2.25 to 3.68 million GPU-hours. This range reflects differences in the historical sample and model assumptions. It should not be interpreted as a statistical prediction interval or as validated lower and upper limits for future GPU requirements.

The naïve benchmark's favourable rolling-origin performance also requires caution. Although it achieved the lowest errors over the two evaluation years, this does not establish that GPU demand will remain constant through 2030. Similarly, the higher projections from the trend models do not provide reliable evidence that continued growth will occur.

Unlike overall HPC and CPU demand, no central GPU forecasting model was selected. Formal 80% and 95% prediction intervals were also not reported because the short historical series and uncertainty in the underlying estimates would make these intervals highly dependent on the modelling assumptions.

Following the project review, GPU projections were retained as exploratory findings but excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios. Those initial scenarios instead use the selected overall HPC demand projection and historical Field of Research allocation shares.

This decision reflects the limitations of the available data rather than the importance of GPU computing. More consistent records of GPU requests, allocations, usage and hardware configurations would be needed before GPU-specific forecasts could support infrastructure planning with greater confidence.

Overall, the GPU analysis demonstrates that different growth assumptions and the inclusion of a single recent observation can substantially change longer-term projections. The results are useful for identifying uncertainty and informing future modelling, but they should not be treated as validated estimates of national GPU capacity requirements.

## Field of Research Scenarios

The previous sections presented national HPC and CPU demand projections, alongside exploratory GPU projections, through 2030. However, the national forecast does not show how computing demand might be distributed across research disciplines. This section examines that question using historical Field of Research (FoR) allocation shares.

The available FoR records do not provide a consistent series of demand requests for every research field. Therefore, the scenarios apply historical allocation shares to the selected national HPC demand projection. The results are illustrative distributions of projected national demand, not independently estimated forecasts of demand within individual research fields.

### Scenario Construction

Three historical reference periods were considered:

1. **Earlier period (2014–2020):** The allocation composition recorded before 2021.
2. **Recent period (2021–2026):** The latest six years of allocation records.
3. **Full period (2014–2026):** The allocation composition across the complete historical series.

The scenario construction followed four steps. First, reported FoR categories were consolidated into nine analytical groups, as described in Section 4.1. Second, annual allocation shares were calculated for each reported group. Third, the mean of the available annual shares was calculated within each reference period and normalised to produce weights totalling 100%. Finally, these weights were applied to the selected national HPC demand projections for 2027–2030.

The calculation is:

$$
D_{f,t}^{(s)} = \widehat{D}_{t} \times w_f^{(s)}
$$

where $D_{f,t}^{(s)}$ represents the illustrative demand for research field $f$ in year $t$ under scenario $s$, $\widehat{D}_{t}$ is the national HPC demand projection, and $w_f^{(s)}$ is the normalised historical allocation share.

The normalisation is calculated as:

$$
w_f^{(s)} =
\frac{\overline{a}_f^{(s)}}
{\sum_j \overline{a}_j^{(s)}}
$$

where $\overline{a}_f^{(s)}$ is the mean observed annual allocation share for research field $f$ during reference period $s$. The denominator sums the mean shares across the nine groups.

This method gives equal weight to each available annual observation within a research field, rather than giving more weight to years with larger total allocations. Missing categories are not treated as confirmed zero allocations. Normalisation ensures that the weights sum to 100%, but it does not correct incomplete historical reporting.

The weights are held constant throughout 2027–2030. This isolates the effect of choosing different historical allocation compositions without introducing additional assumptions about future changes in research-field shares.

### Historical Allocation Assumptions

@fig-for-scenario-comparison compares the normalised allocation shares for the three reference periods. All nine research-field groups are included.


```{r}
#| label: fig-for-scenario-comparison
#| fig-cap: "Normalised Field of Research allocation shares across three historical reference periods."
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 7.5
#| out-width: 100%
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(scales)

# Prepare historical FoR allocation data
for_scenario_source <- for_plot_data |>
  transmute(
    year = as.integer(year),
    for_group = as.character(for_visual_group),
    allocation_share = as.numeric(allocation_share)
  ) |>
  filter(
    year >= 2014,
    year <= 2026,
    !is.na(for_group),
    is.finite(allocation_share)
  )

stopifnot(
  identical(
    sort(unique(for_scenario_source$year)),
    2014:2026
  ),
  all(for_scenario_source$allocation_share >= 0)
)

# Calculate normalised allocation weights
make_for_weights <- function(data, start_year, end_year,
                             period_label) {
  data |>
    filter(
      year >= start_year,
      year <= end_year
    ) |>
    group_by(for_group) |>
    summarise(
      mean_share = mean(allocation_share),
      years_reported = n_distinct(year),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    mutate(
      scenario_share = mean_share / sum(mean_share),
      period = period_label
    )
}

# Three historical reference periods
for_scenario_weights <- bind_rows(
  make_for_weights(
    for_scenario_source, 2014, 2020,
    "Earlier (2014–2020)"
  ),
  make_for_weights(
    for_scenario_source, 2021, 2026,
    "Recent (2021–2026)"
  ),
  make_for_weights(
    for_scenario_source, 2014, 2026,
    "Full period (2014–2026)"
  )
)

# Verify that each scenario sums to 100%
for_weight_check <- for_scenario_weights |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    total_share = sum(scenario_share),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stopifnot(
  all(abs(for_weight_check$total_share - 1) < 1e-10)
)

# Set the order of historical periods
for_scenario_weights <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    period = factor(
      period,
      levels = c(
        "Earlier (2014–2020)",
        "Recent (2021–2026)",
        "Full period (2014–2026)"
      )
    )
  )

# Order research fields by their largest allocation share
for_group_order <- for_scenario_weights |>
  group_by(for_group) |>
  summarise(
    max_share = max(scenario_share),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  arrange(max_share) |>
  pull(for_group)

for_scenario_weights <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    for_group = factor(
      for_group,
      levels = for_group_order
    )
  )

# Create the revised chart
ggplot(
  for_scenario_weights,
  aes(
    x = scenario_share,
    y = for_group,
    fill = period
  )
) +
  geom_col(
    position = position_dodge(width = 0.8),
    width = 0.72
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Earlier (2014–2020)" = "#64748B",
      "Recent (2021–2026)" = "#0077A8",
      "Full period (2014–2026)" = "#D97706"
    )
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(
    labels = label_percent(accuracy = 1),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.08))
  ) +
  labs(
    x = "Normalised historical allocation share",
    y = NULL,
    fill = NULL,
    caption = paste(
      "Weights use observed-year means.",
      "Historical category coverage and reporting differ."
    )
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
  theme(
    legend.position = "bottom",
    legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
    legend.key.width = grid::unit(1.5, "cm"),
    axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10),
    axis.title.x = element_text(size = 11),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 9)
  )
```


@tbl-for-weights reports the normalised scenario weights for all nine research-field groups. The number of reported years is also included to show where the historical coverage differs.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-for-weights
#| tbl-cap: "Normalised FoR allocation weights and reporting coverage across the three historical reference periods."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

for_weights_table <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    for_group = as.character(for_group),
    period = as.character(period),
    share_label = sprintf(
      "%.2f%% (%d)",
      100 * scenario_share,
      years_reported
    )
  ) |>
  select(
    for_group,
    period,
    share_label
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = share_label
  ) |>
  arrange(
    for_group
  )

knitr::kable(
  for_weights_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Research field",
    "Earlier (2014–2020)",
    "Recent (2021–2026)",
    "Full period (2014–2026)"
  )
)
```

*Note: Each cell shows the normalised allocation weight followed by the number of years with reported observations in parentheses. The reference periods contain seven, six and thirteen years respectively. Percentages are normalised within each period.*

The earlier-period scenario gives the largest allocation weight to Earth and Environmental Sciences at approximately 30.38%. Chemical Sciences follows at 18.28%, with Physical Sciences and Engineering and Technology accounting for 16.26% and 16.24% respectively.

The recent-period composition differs considerably. Engineering and Technology becomes the largest group at 33.28%, followed by Physical Sciences (21.11%), Chemical Sciences (17.02%) and Earth and Environmental Sciences (13.36%).

Engineering and Technology therefore gains approximately 17.04 percentage points between the earlier and recent scenarios. Over the same comparison, Earth and Environmental Sciences loses approximately 17.02 percentage points.

The full-period weights lie between these two compositions for the major research fields. Engineering and Technology accounts for approximately 24.19%, Earth and Environmental Sciences for 22.55%, Physical Sciences for 18.55% and Chemical Sciences for 17.74%.

Reporting coverage also differs across research fields. For example, the recent-period weight for Unclassified and Operational is based on only two reported years, while most major research fields have observations for all six years. Social Sciences, Humanities and Built Environment has only five reported years across the full period. Because the weights are calculated from available observations, groups with incomplete coverage may not represent the entire reference period.

These differences should not automatically be interpreted as changes in underlying research demand. The historical records span the FoR 2008 and FoR 2020 classification systems. In addition, the 2017 Pawsey-wide reporting scope differs from other observations, while the completeness of category reporting varies across years.

The normalised weights therefore provide a consistent calculation method for comparing the constructed scenarios, but they do not remove differences in classification, facility coverage or reporting completeness. Nor do they establish that research priorities or computing requirements changed by the same percentages.

### Illustrative Distribution of Demand in 2030

The three historical allocation compositions were applied to the same selected national HPC demand projection.

The central linear model projects approximately 2.50 million kSU in 2030. Each scenario distributes this national total across the nine research-field groups using its corresponding normalised weights.

@tbl-for-2030 presents the resulting distributions. Calculations use the unrounded national forecast.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-for-2030
#| tbl-cap: "Illustrative 2030 HPC demand distribution under three historical FoR allocation scenarios, in kSU."
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false

stopifnot(exists("overall_linear"))

hpc_2030_ksu <- as.numeric(
  predict(
    overall_linear,
    newdata = data.frame(
      year = 2030,
      time = 2030 - 2014
    )
  )
)

stopifnot(
  length(hpc_2030_ksu) == 1,
  is.finite(hpc_2030_ksu),
  hpc_2030_ksu > 0
)

for_2030_results <- for_scenario_weights |>
  mutate(
    projected_ksu = hpc_2030_ksu * scenario_share
  )

for_2030_check <- for_2030_results |>
  group_by(period) |>
  summarise(
    scenario_total = sum(projected_ksu),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

stopifnot(
  all(
    abs(
      for_2030_check$scenario_total - hpc_2030_ksu
    ) < 1e-6
  )
)

for_2030_table <- for_2030_results |>
  mutate(
    for_group = as.character(for_group),
    period = as.character(period)
  ) |>
  select(
    for_group,
    period,
    projected_ksu
  ) |>
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = projected_ksu
  ) |>
  arrange(
    desc(`Recent (2021–2026)`)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    across(
      where(is.numeric),
      ~ format(
        round(.x),
        big.mark = ",",
        trim = TRUE,
        scientific = FALSE
      )
    )
  )

knitr::kable(
  for_2030_table,
  col.names = c(
    "Research field",
    "Earlier (2014–2020)",
    "Recent (2021–2026)",
    "Full period (2014–2026)"
  )
)
```

The choice of historical reference period produces substantial differences in the indicative distribution of national HPC demand. The national forecast remains unchanged between scenarios; only the assumed distribution differs.

Under the recent-period scenario, Engineering and Technology accounts for approximately 832,908 kSU in 2030, compared with 406,401 kSU under the earlier-period scenario. This is a difference of 426,507 kSU, even though both scenarios use the same national demand projection.

Earth and Environmental Sciences shows the opposite pattern. Its indicative allocation decreases from 760,374 kSU under the earlier-period scenario to 334,353 kSU under the recent-period scenario, a difference of 426,021 kSU.

Under the recent-period scenario, Physical Sciences accounts for approximately 528,466 kSU, while Chemical Sciences accounts for 425,998 kSU. The corresponding full-period estimates are 464,339 kSU and 443,903 kSU, respectively.

These differences arise entirely from the historical allocation weights applied to the same national forecast. The choice of reference period is therefore an important modelling assumption, not merely a presentation choice.

The figures should not be interpreted as confirmed future allocations or direct forecasts of researcher demand. They are conditional estimates showing how the national forecast would be distributed if each historical allocation composition were maintained.

### Interpretation and Planning Implications

The three scenarios provide different views of how projected national HPC demand might be distributed.

The earlier-period scenario reflects a composition in which Earth and Environmental Sciences received a larger share of allocations. The recent-period scenario places greater weight on Engineering and Technology. The full-period scenario provides a broader historical reference, although it remains affected by reporting differences across the complete series.

The results also demonstrate an important limitation of using allocation records as a proxy for demand. Allocations reflect computing resources made available through allocation processes, which may be lower than the resources requested or required by researchers. Therefore, the indicative distributions should not be interpreted as direct measures of future research-field demand.

The FoR classification change and differences in facility reporting also limit how confidently historical shifts can be attributed to changes in research activity.

For national HPC planning, the main implication is that the assumed research-field composition can materially change the indicative distribution of a fixed national forecast. The difference of approximately 426,500 kSU for Engineering and Technology illustrates this sensitivity. Comparing alternative reference periods makes the uncertainty more visible than selecting one historical composition as definitive.

More consistent FoR-level records of requested, allocated and used computing resources would support stronger future analysis. A validated mapping between historical classification systems and more complete reporting across facilities would also improve the reliability of research-field comparisons.

Overall, the FoR scenarios extend the selected national HPC forecast by showing how different historical allocation assumptions affect its illustrative distribution. They provide a basis for examining planning sensitivity, but they do not establish independently validated forecasts of future demand for individual research fields.

## Summary of Results

The historical analysis identified increasing pressure between recorded HPC demand and available allocations. In 2026, recorded HPC demand reached approximately 2.24 million kSU, while allocations were approximately 872,000 kSU. This represented a fulfilment rate of 38.9%, indicating that recorded requests substantially exceeded allocated resources.

The rolling-origin evaluation identified the linear trend as the preferred central model as the central forecasting model for overall HPC and CPU demand. By 2030, these models project approximately 2.50 million kSU and 1.37 billion CPU core-hours, respectively. Alternative growth assumptions produce substantially different projections, particularly under the log-linear models. The results are also sensitive to the inclusion of the 2026 observation.

GPU forecasting remained exploratory because only five annual modelling observations were available. The five scenarios produced 2030 estimates ranging from approximately 2.25 to 3.68 million GPU-hours. No central GPU forecast was selected, and these projections were excluded from the initial national HPC planning scenarios.

The FoR scenarios demonstrated that the indicative distribution of projected national demand depends strongly on historical allocation assumptions. Engineering and Technology accounted for 16.24% of the earlier-period scenario compared with 33.28% of the recent-period scenario. Applying these weights to the same national forecast produced a difference of approximately 426,500 kSU in its illustrative 2030 demand distribution.

Together, these findings show that forecasting results depend not only on historical model accuracy but also on data coverage, measurement assumptions, growth specifications and scenario construction. Their implications for national HPC planning are discussed in the following chapter.

# Discussion

## Interpretation of the Main Findings

The analysis identified three main findings: recorded HPC demand has grown faster than available allocations, longer-term forecasts are sensitive to modelling assumptions, and the distribution of projected demand across research fields depends on the historical allocation period used.

### Growing Difference Between Demand and Allocation

The historical analysis showed a substantial difference between requested and allocated HPC resources. In 2026, recorded demand reached approximately 2.24 million kSU, while allocations were approximately 872,000 kSU. This resulted in a fulfilment rate of 38.9%, indicating that less than half of the recorded requests were allocated.

This difference is important because increasing demand does not necessarily result in a corresponding increase in available computing resources. If requests continue growing while allocations remain constrained, the gap between the two measures could become more pronounced.

However, the recorded gap should not be interpreted as a complete measure of unmet national research demand. Researchers may adjust their applications according to expected availability, while others may choose not to apply because of capacity limitations. The available records also do not show whether all requested resources would have been used if allocated.

Therefore, the historical results provide evidence of pressure within the reported allocation system, rather than a direct estimate of the total computing capacity required by Australian researchers.

### Interpretation of the Forecasting Results

The rolling-origin evaluation identified the linear trend as the preferred central model for overall HPC and CPU demand. These models provided competitive historical accuracy without assuming that proportional growth would continue indefinitely.

The selected models project approximately 2.50 million kSU of overall HPC demand and 1.37 billion CPU core-hours by 2030. Both projections indicate continued growth, although their interpretation depends on the historical measures used to construct the datasets.

The alternative scenarios demonstrate why the central forecasts should not be treated as the only possible outcomes. For overall HPC demand, excluding the 2026 observation reduces the 2030 projection from approximately 2.50 million to 2.29 million kSU. The full-history log-linear model produces a substantially higher projection of approximately 6.48 million kSU.

CPU demand shows a similar sensitivity. The linear model projects approximately 1.37 billion core-hours in 2030, compared with approximately 2.48 billion under the full-history log-linear model.

An important difference is that the log-linear model performed poorly relative to the linear model for overall HPC demand, while the two approaches performed similarly for CPU demand. Consequently, the higher CPU scenario cannot be dismissed solely on the basis of historical forecast accuracy. Nevertheless, competitive one-year-ahead performance does not establish that proportional growth will continue through 2030.

These findings show that model selection involves more than choosing the lowest historical forecast error. The assumed growth pattern becomes increasingly important as the forecasting horizon extends.

The statistical prediction intervals provide another perspective on uncertainty. For 2030, the selected overall HPC model has a 95% prediction interval of approximately 1.98–3.03 million kSU, while the corresponding CPU interval is approximately 974–1,766 million core-hours. These intervals are conditional on the fitted linear models and do not include uncertainty arising from alternative growth specifications, historical conversions or future technological changes.

### GPU Demand and Research Field Differences

GPU forecasting presented a different challenge. The modelling dataset contained only five annual observations from 2022 to 2026, and the rolling-origin evaluation covered just two years. Although the naïve benchmark achieved the lowest forecast errors, this provides insufficient evidence that GPU demand will remain constant.

The five exploratory scenarios produced 2030 projections ranging from approximately 2.25 to 3.68 million GPU-hours. The substantial difference between models fitted with and without 2026 demonstrates the influence of a single recent observation on such a short series.

For this reason, no central GPU forecast was selected. The scenarios are useful for understanding sensitivity to modelling assumptions, but they are not sufficiently reliable to support specific GPU capacity requirements.

The Field of Research (FoR) analysis identified a different source of uncertainty. Engineering and Technology accounted for 16.24% of the earlier-period allocation scenario but 33.28% of the recent-period scenario. When these weights were applied to the same 2030 national HPC demand projection, the indicative distribution for this field differed by approximately 426,500 kSU.

Earth and Environmental Sciences showed the opposite pattern, receiving a considerably greater share under the earlier-period scenario.

These differences demonstrate that the choice of historical reference period can substantially affect the indicative distribution of projected national demand. However, they cannot establish that underlying research demand changed by the same proportions, particularly given the changes in FoR classification and historical reporting coverage.

## Implications for National HPC Planning

### Planning for Growth and Uncertainty

The central forecasts provide a quantitative reference for considering future national HPC requirements. However, planning should not depend on a single projected value for 2030.

For overall HPC demand, the selected linear model projects approximately 2.50 million kSU, while alternative assumptions produce substantially different results. This suggests that infrastructure planning should examine a range of possible demand outcomes rather than assuming that the central trajectory will occur exactly as estimated.

The distinction between prediction intervals and alternative growth scenarios is particularly important. Prediction intervals describe uncertainty conditional on a selected statistical model, whereas alternative scenarios demonstrate how different historical samples or growth assumptions change the projected demand.

Both forms of uncertainty are relevant, but neither captures every factor affecting future infrastructure requirements.

The historical difference between requested and allocated resources also needs to be considered. Projected demand alone does not show how much additional capacity is necessary because the available records do not establish a direct relationship between requested kSU, allocated resources and actual usage.

Consequently, the forecasts are most suitable as inputs to planning discussions and further capacity assessments, rather than direct specifications for infrastructure investment.

### Accounting for Changes in Computing Technology

Another important consideration is that HPC demand is reported using different accounting measures.

Overall HPC demand is expressed in kSU, while CPU and GPU demand are represented using core-hours and GPU-hours. These measures describe different aspects of computing activity and should not be added together or treated as directly interchangeable.

Changes in hardware performance, system configurations and service-unit conversion factors can also affect the relationship between reported demand and physical computing capacity.

For example, a future computing system may deliver greater performance per core-hour than an earlier system. Similarly, changes in GPU architectures could affect the resources needed to complete comparable research workloads.

This means that an increase in reported computing demand does not necessarily translate into an identical percentage increase in physical infrastructure requirements.

National planning would therefore benefit from combining demand projections with information about system performance, resource utilisation, workload characteristics and expected technological changes.

### Considering Research Field Requirements

The FoR scenarios provide an additional perspective by illustrating how the same national HPC projection can be distributed differently across research disciplines.

The recent-period scenario gives greater weight to Engineering and Technology, while the earlier-period scenario gives greater weight to Earth and Environmental Sciences. These differences may be useful when examining how historical allocation patterns influence indicative future resource distributions.

However, allocation shares are not direct measures of research demand. They reflect resources made available through historical allocation processes and may be affected by capacity constraints, reporting practices and classification changes.

For this reason, the FoR scenarios should not be used as fixed allocation targets or as evidence that particular disciplines will require the projected amounts.

Instead, they provide a basis for discussing distributional sensitivity and identifying where more detailed research-field demand information would improve planning.

## Limitations and Future Work

### Data Availability and Historical Comparability

The main limitation of the analysis is the short and uneven historical record.

Overall HPC and CPU demand were modelled using 13 annual observations from 2014 to 2026. Although sufficient to compare simple forecasting methods, this provides limited information for estimating longer-term growth patterns or identifying structural changes.

GPU forecasting was more restricted, with only five annual modelling observations. The limited evaluation period prevented a reliable comparison of long-term forecasting performance.

Historical comparability also presented challenges. The source records covered different facilities, computing systems and reporting conventions. Resource conversions were required to construct consistent analytical measures, and some GPU estimates depended on allocation shares and working assumptions.

Although these assumptions were documented, they introduce measurement uncertainty that is not fully represented in the statistical forecast intervals.

The FoR analysis was also affected by differences between the 2008 and 2020 classification systems, changes in reporting coverage and the inclusion of records with different facility scopes.

Normalisation allowed historical allocation shares to be compared across the constructed scenarios, but it did not remove these underlying differences.

### Forecasting and Scenario Limitations

The forecasting methods were intentionally simple because of the limited annual observations.

Linear and log-linear models provide interpretable representations of historical growth, but they cannot directly account for future changes in research funding, computing technology, national policy or facility capacity.

The rolling-origin evaluation assessed one-year-ahead forecasting performance. Strong performance over this horizon does not necessarily imply reliable projections four years into the future.

The results were also sensitive to the 2026 observation. This was particularly evident in the alternative HPC, CPU and GPU scenarios, demonstrating that a single recent year can materially influence longer-term projections.

Furthermore, the model-based prediction intervals depend on the assumptions of the selected linear models. They do not account for uncertainty in historical reconstruction, future technology or the choice between alternative forecasting specifications.

The FoR scenarios have a separate limitation because they distribute national demand using historical allocation shares rather than independently forecasting demand within each research field.

### Recommendations for Future Work

Future analysis could be strengthened through several improvements:

1. **Improve requested, allocated and used resource records.** Consistent annual data across facilities would make it possible to examine the relationship between applications, allocations and actual utilisation more directly.

2. **Validate resource conversion factors.** Further consultation with facility operators could improve the consistency of historical kSU, CPU and GPU measures, particularly where hardware configurations or accounting rules changed.

3. **Extend the GPU demand series.** More detailed GPU request, allocation and usage records would support stronger evaluation and help determine whether a separate GPU forecasting model is appropriate.

4. **Improve FoR-level demand information.** Consistent research-field request data and validated classification mappings would allow demand to be modelled directly rather than approximated using historical allocation shares.

5. **Update and evaluate forecasts regularly.** As new annual observations become available, the models should be re-estimated and their forecast performance reassessed. This would also help determine whether the linear trends remain appropriate.

6. **Connect demand projections with infrastructure characteristics.** Combining forecasting results with hardware performance, utilisation and expected technology changes would provide a stronger basis for translating reported computing demand into practical capacity requirements.

Overall, the project provides a documented and reproducible basis for examining historical national HPC demand and its possible development through 2030. Its main contribution is not a single definitive capacity estimate, but a comparison of plausible projections, their underlying assumptions and the limitations of the available evidence.

These findings can support national HPC planning discussions while identifying the additional data required for more reliable future assessments.

# Conclusion

This project assembled and standardised publicly available Australian national research HPC records covering 2014–2026 and developed demand projections through 2030. The analysis combined historical data reconstruction, resource conversion, descriptive analysis, rolling-origin forecast evaluation and scenario development. It also documented the assumptions and limitations associated with using publicly reported computing data.

The historical analysis identified a substantial difference between requested and allocated HPC resources. In 2026, recorded demand reached approximately 2.24 million kSU, compared with allocations of approximately 872,000 kSU, representing a fulfilment rate of 38.9%. This finding indicates increasing pressure within the reported allocation system, although the difference cannot be treated as a complete measure of unmet national research demand.

The forecasting evaluation selected linear trend models as the central approach for overall HPC and CPU demand. By 2030, these models project approximately 2.50 million kSU of overall HPC demand and 1.37 billion CPU core-hours. Alternative models and the exclusion of the 2026 observation produced substantially different projections, demonstrating the importance of historical data coverage and growth assumptions when interpreting longer-term forecasts.

GPU projections remained exploratory because only five annual modelling observations were available. The Field of Research scenarios also demonstrated that the indicative distribution of future national HPC demand depends on the historical allocation period selected. These findings highlight the need to distinguish between modelled demand, historical allocations and actual computing capacity.

The main contribution of this project is a reproducible analytical framework that brings together historical data, documented conversion assumptions, forecast evaluation and scenario analysis. The results provide the Australian Academy of Science with an evidence-based reference for discussing future national HPC requirements, while making the uncertainty and data limitations clear. The accompanying Quarto documentation and Git repository preserve the detailed methods and calculations for future review and updates.
